fig.cap: Higher MZ than DZ concordance points to genes; MZ concordance well below 100% points to environment.
fig.alt: Schizophrenia concordance in MZ twins, DZ twins and the general population.
fig.credit: This graph was originally developed for the 520 Quest app. Approximate literature values (question data).

ox: Correct. MZ twins share nearly all their genes. If they match more often than DZ twins, even though they grew up apart and the DZ twins grew up together, genes are the best explanation. So genetic factors contribute to differences in the trait.
Not quite. The MZ twins were raised in different homes, so they didn't share a family environment at all. That can't explain why they match more. And the DZ twins, who did share a home, matched less.

Not quite. This result shows genes contribute, not that genes are everything. If the trait were fully genetic, MZ twins would match close to 100% of the time. Real studies almost never find that, so environment still matters.
Not quite. Random errors during development happen by chance, so they would make twins less alike, not more. They can't explain a steady pattern of identical twins matching more often.

p: Monozygotic (MZ) twins come from one fertilized egg and share nearly 100% of their genes. Dizygotic (DZ) twins come from two eggs and share about 50%, like ordinary siblings. Concordance is how often both twins have a trait when one does.

If MZ twins match more than DZ twins, genes likely contribute to the trait. Studying identical twins raised apart is extra powerful, because it removes the shared home as an explanation. Still, a genetic influence isn't the same as genetic destiny.

mem: MZ: about 100% shared genes; DZ: about 50%
MZ matching more than DZ means genes contribute
Raised apart rules out a shared home
Genetic influence doesn't mean genes decide everything
d_7A_1.trap: Treating a genetic influence as meaning genes alone decide the trait.
d_7A_1.plain: If two copies of the same recipe turn out very similar cakes in two different kitchens, the recipe clearly matters a lot.

fig.cap: Theories of emotion differ in order: arousal first (James-Lange), simultaneous (Cannon-Bard), arousal plus label (Schachter-Singer), appraisal first (Lazarus).
fig.alt: Flow diagrams of four theories of emotion.
fig.credit: This diagram was originally developed for the 520 Quest app.

ox: Not quite. The James-Lange theory says your body's reaction comes first, and noticing that reaction is the emotion. With no labeling step, it would predict the same emotion from the same shot. It can't explain why some people felt angry and others felt happy.
Correct. Two-factor theory says emotion equals body arousal plus a cognitive label. The shot supplied the arousal, and the confederate's angry or giddy behavior supplied the label.

Not quite. The Cannon-Bard theory says arousal and emotion happen at the same time and independently. It doesn't say emotion comes first, and it doesn't include reading cues from the situation, which is what drove the results here.

Not quite. The facial feedback hypothesis says your facial expressions can shape your emotions, like smiling making you feel a little happier. This study changed body arousal and social cues, not faces.

p: Two-factor theory says an emotion needs two things: physical arousal and a mental label that explains it. You get the label by looking around at the situation.

In the study, everyone got the same epinephrine, so their arousal was the same. People next to an angry confederate felt anger; people next to a cheerful one felt euphoria. Compare the other theories: James-Lange says arousal comes first and is the emotion, and Cannon-Bard says arousal and emotion happen at the same time.

mem: Two-factor: emotion = arousal + label
Schachter-Singer epinephrine study
James-Lange: arousal first, then emotion
Cannon-Bard: both at the same time
d_7A_14.trap: Ignoring the confederate. The situation supplying the label is the whole point.
d_7A_14.plain: Your heart pounds. On a roller coaster you call it excitement. In a dark alley you call it fear. Same heartbeat, different label.

ox: Correct. Dissociative identity disorder involves two or more distinct identities or personality states, plus memory gaps for everyday events that go beyond ordinary forgetting.

Not quite. Borderline personality disorder involves unstable mood, relationships and sense of self. The person's self-image may shift, but they don't have separate identities with memory gaps between them.
Not quite. This is the classic mix-up. Schizophrenia is a psychotic disorder: hallucinations, delusions and disorganized thinking. Despite the name, it isn't split personality.
Not quite. Schizoid personality disorder means being detached from relationships and showing little emotion. It doesn't involve separate identities or memory gaps.

p: Dissociative disorders involve a break in memory, awareness or sense of identity. In dissociative identity disorder, once called multiple personality disorder, a person has two or more distinct identities that take turns being in control.
The memory gaps are more than normal forgetting and often cover everyday events, not just trauma. Related disorders include dissociative amnesia, which is memory loss without separate identities.

mem: DID: multiple identities + memory gaps
Schizophrenia is not split personality
Dissociative amnesia is a related disorder
d_7A_25.trap: Treating schizophrenia as split personality. Schizophrenia is about losing touch with reality, not having several identities.
d_7A_25.plain: It's like one phone shared by two people, each with their own account, and neither can see the other's messages.

fig.cap: Mesolimbic = reward (excess linked to positive symptoms); mesocortical = cognition (deficit linked to negative symptoms); nigrostriatal = movement; tuberoinfundibular = prolactin.
fig.alt: Four dopamine pathways from the VTA, substantia nigra and hypothalamus.
fig.credit: This diagram was originally developed for the 520 Quest app.

ox: Not quite. The neuromuscular junction is where a nerve tells a muscle to contract, using acetylcholine. Too little acetylcholine signaling there causes muscle weakness, as in myasthenia gravis. It doesn't cause hallucinations.
Not quite. GABA is a calming messenger. Losing its braking effect in the spinal cord makes muscles spasm and stiffen, like in tetanus. It isn't linked to psychosis.

Correct. The dopamine hypothesis links positive symptoms, like hallucinations and delusions, to too much dopamine activity in the mesolimbic pathway. Antipsychotic drugs block D₂ dopamine receptors, which backs up this idea.
Not quite. The raphe nuclei are the brainstem's serotonin centers, and low serotonin is linked to depression, not to the dopamine hypothesis. The word 'only' is also a warning sign.

p: Positive symptoms of schizophrenia are things added to normal experience, like hallucinations and delusions. Negative symptoms are things taken away, like flat emotion and low motivation. The dopamine hypothesis focuses on the positive ones.

It says positive symptoms come from too much dopamine activity in the mesolimbic pathway. The main evidence: antipsychotics block D₂ dopamine receptors and reduce these symptoms, while drugs that raise dopamine can trigger psychosis.

mem: Positive symptoms: too much dopamine, mesolimbic
Antipsychotics block D₂ receptors
Parkinson's: too little dopamine
d_7A_3.trap: Mixing up Parkinson's (too little dopamine) with schizophrenia (too much).
d_7A_3.plain: It's like a radio with the volume cranked way up. The brain hears its own signals so loudly it picks up voices that aren't there.

ox: Correct. Antisocial personality disorder is a long-term pattern of lying, violating others' rights and showing no remorse. It's in Cluster B.
Not quite. Avoidant personality disorder means feeling inadequate and avoiding people out of fear of rejection. That's nearly the opposite of someone who walks over others' rights.
Not quite. Dependent personality disorder means an excessive need to be taken care of, clinging and giving in to others. It doesn't involve lying and harming people without guilt.

Not quite. Obsessive-compulsive personality disorder means perfectionism, rules and rigid control. Those people may be stubborn, but they don't typically lie and violate others' rights without remorse.

p: Personality disorders are lasting patterns of thinking and behaving that cause problems in life. They're sorted into three clusters: A (odd or eccentric), B (dramatic or impulsive) and C (anxious or fearful).

Antisocial personality disorder is in Cluster B. It involves lying, rule-breaking, impulsive or aggressive behavior, and no remorse. A diagnosis requires the person to be at least 18, with signs of conduct problems starting before age 15.

mem: Antisocial: lying, rights violations, no remorse
Cluster B: antisocial, borderline, histrionic, narcissistic
Avoidant and dependent: Cluster C (anxious)
d_7A_37.trap: Picking avoidant or dependent just because they're also personality disorders. Lying and no remorse mean antisocial.
d_7A_37.plain: Think of a kid who breaks the rules, lies about it, and shrugs when someone gets hurt.

ox: Correct. Displacement redirects an impulse (anger at the boss) toward a safer target (the dog).
Projection means putting your own unwanted feelings onto someone else, such as 'you are angry at me'.
Reaction formation means acting the opposite of how you feel, such as being extra nice to someone you dislike.
Sublimation means turning an impulse into something socially acceptable, like using anger for sports.

p: Defense mechanisms are unconscious ways the mind handles uncomfortable feelings. Displacement moves a feeling from the real source to a safer target.
The boss is risky to yell at, so the dog gets it.

mem: Displacement: safer target.
Projection: blame feelings on others.
Reaction formation: do the opposite.
Sublimation: channel into good outlets.
q102.trap: Confusing displacement (same feeling, new target) with sublimation (same feeling, healthy outlet).
q102.plain: You are mad at your sister but you slam your door and yell at your teddy bear.

ox: Correct. Yerkes-Dodson is an inverted U. Performance peaks at a moderate arousal level, and the peak sits lower for hard (complex) tasks.
Wrong. Very high arousal (panic, extreme stress) makes performance drop. The trap is thinking more energy always means better results.
Wrong. Very low arousal means boredom and poor focus, so performance is low. The trap is thinking calm is always best.
Wrong. The whole law says arousal does change performance, in an inverted-U shape.

p: Arousal means how alert and activated your body and brain are. The Yerkes-Dodson law says performance is best at a moderate level of arousal. Too little and you are bored. Too much and you are overwhelmed.
The best level depends on the task. Hard tasks do best with lower arousal. Easy or well-practiced tasks do best with higher arousal.

mem: Performance vs arousal is an inverted U
Moderate arousal is best
Complex tasks peak at lower arousal; simple tasks peak at higher arousal
q103.trap: Choosing 'as high as possible' because motivation sounds good. The law is about a middle sweet spot.
q103.plain: Think of a guitar string: too loose and it makes no sound, too tight and it snaps, just right sounds good.

fig.cap: Performance peaks at moderate arousal; the optimum is higher for simple tasks.
fig.alt: Inverted-U curves of performance against arousal.
fig.credit: This graph was originally developed for the 520 Quest app. Schematic curves.

ox: Correct. The smoker holds two conflicting ideas: smoking is harmful, and I smoke. Dismissing the studies changes the belief to match the behavior, which lowers the discomfort. That is cognitive dissonance reduction.
Wrong. Fundamental attribution error is blaming other people's behavior on their personality and ignoring the situation. This is about the smoker's own conflict, not judging others.

Wrong. Confirmation bias is favoring information that agrees with what you already believe. It may play a part, but the key feature here is easing the clash between belief and behavior. The word 'only' is the trap.
Wrong. Self-efficacy is your belief in your own ability to succeed at a task. Nothing here is about ability.

p: Cognitive dissonance is the unpleasant tension you feel when your beliefs and your actions do not match. People want to remove that tension.
They can change the behavior, change the belief, or add a new belief that excuses the behavior. Calling the health studies exaggerated is changing the belief to fit the action.

mem: Dissonance = belief and behavior conflict, causing discomfort
Ways to reduce: change behavior, change belief, add excuse
Fundamental attribution error is about judging OTHERS
Self-efficacy = belief in your own ability
q104.trap: Picking confirmation bias. Look for the clash between what someone knows and what they do.
q104.plain: You eat a whole cake while on a diet and say 'it was a small cake anyway.' You changed the story to feel better.

fig.cap: ELM: central route (argument quality) when motivated and able, peripheral route (cues) otherwise. TPB: attitude, subjective norms and perceived control shape intention.
fig.alt: Elaboration likelihood model and theory of planned behavior.
fig.credit: This diagram was originally developed for the 520 Quest app.

ox: Correct. 'I didn't study enough' puts the cause inside the person (own effort), which is an internal locus of control.
Wrong. Luck is outside your control, so this is an external locus. The trap is that it sounds like a personal statement because it says 'I'.
Wrong. Blaming the professor puts the cause on another person, so it is external.
Wrong. Test difficulty is a feature of the situation, so it is external.

p: Locus of control is where you believe the causes of outcomes lie. Internal means you think your own actions and effort cause results. External means you think luck, other people, or the situation cause them.
Ask one question: is the cause inside me or outside me?

mem: Internal = my effort, my choices
External = luck, fate, other people, situation
Internal locus is linked with more persistence and better coping
q105.trap: Every option starts with 'I failed because', but only the one naming your own action is internal.
q105.plain: If you lose a game and say 'I should have practiced,' that is internal. If you say 'the referee cheated,' that is external.

ox: Correct. Identical twins share nearly all their genes. If they are alike even in different homes, genes likely play a big role in the trait.
Wrong. If the environment alone made the trait, twins in different homes should differ. They are similar, so this does not fit.
Wrong. One finding cannot show genes are the only cause. Heritability is almost never 100 percent, and environment still matters. 'Entirely' and 'fully' are the traps.
Wrong. The twins were raised apart, so they did not share a family environment.

p: Identical (monozygotic) twins come from one egg and share almost all their genes. Studying them when raised apart separates genes from shared family environment.
High similarity in different environments points to genetic influence. It does not prove genes are the only influence.

mem: Identical twins share about 100% of genes; fraternal about 50%
Twins raised apart test genes vs environment
Similar when apart means substantial genetic contribution, not total
q106.trap: Absolute words like 'entirely' or 'fully determined' are almost always wrong in behavior genetics.
q106.plain: Two copies of the same recipe baked in different kitchens come out tasting alike, so the recipe matters a lot.

fig.cap: Higher MZ than DZ concordance points to genes; MZ concordance well below 100% points to environment.
fig.alt: Schizophrenia concordance in MZ twins, DZ twins and the general population.
fig.credit: This graph was originally developed for the 520 Quest app. Approximate literature values (question data).

fig.cap: Mesolimbic = reward (excess linked to positive symptoms); mesocortical = cognition (deficit linked to negative symptoms); nigrostriatal = movement; tuberoinfundibular = prolactin.
fig.alt: Four dopamine pathways from the VTA, substantia nigra and hypothalamus.
fig.credit: This diagram was originally developed for the 520 Quest app.

ox: Correct. Dopamine neurons in the ventral tegmental area send signals to the nucleus accumbens, and that circuit is the reward pathway. Addictive drugs raise dopamine there, so the brain learns 'that was great, do it again.' That's what reinforcement means.
Not quite. Acetylcholine is the messenger that tells muscles to contract, and in the brain it helps with attention and memory. It isn't the core reward signal that addictive drugs hijack.
Not quite. Glycine is an inhibitory messenger, meaning it makes neurons less likely to fire. It works mostly in the spinal cord and brainstem, far from the reward pathway.

Not quite. GABA is the brain's main inhibitory messenger. This one is tempting because alcohol, benzodiazepines and other sedatives act on GABA. But calming neurons down isn't the same as rewarding a behavior, and the reward signal itself is dopamine.

p: A neurotransmitter is a chemical messenger one neuron releases to signal the next. The reward pathway, also called the mesolimbic pathway, runs from the ventral tegmental area (VTA) in the midbrain to the nucleus accumbens. The messenger it uses is dopamine.

Food, sex, winning and addictive drugs all raise dopamine in the nucleus accumbens. That burst teaches the brain to repeat whatever caused it. Drugs are so powerful because they push dopamine up harder and faster than natural rewards do.

mem: Reward pathway: VTA to nucleus accumbens
Its messenger: dopamine
Addictive drugs boost dopamine there
GABA and glycine calm neurons down
x7A_001.trap: Picking GABA because alcohol and sedatives act on it. When a question says reward or reinforcement, think dopamine.
x7A_001.plain: Dopamine is the brain's gold star sticker. It says 'good job, do that again,' and drugs hand out stickers by the fistful.

fig.cap: Mesolimbic = reward (excess linked to positive symptoms); mesocortical = cognition (deficit linked to negative symptoms); nigrostriatal = movement; tuberoinfundibular = prolactin.
fig.alt: Four dopamine pathways from the VTA, substantia nigra and hypothalamus.
fig.credit: This diagram was originally developed for the 520 Quest app.

ox: Correct. The nigrostriatal pathway carries dopamine from the substantia nigra to the striatum, part of the brain's movement-control system. Blocking D₂ receptors there takes away the dopamine signal, and you get tremor and stiffness that look like Parkinson disease.

Not quite. The tuberoinfundibular pathway runs from the hypothalamus to the pituitary, where dopamine keeps prolactin (a milk-making hormone) in check. Blocking it raises prolactin, which can cause breast milk production or missed periods. It doesn't cause tremor.

Not quite. The mesocortical pathway carries dopamine to the prefrontal cortex and affects thinking, focus and motivation. Blocking it can make someone flat or unmotivated, but it doesn't make their hands shake.

Not quite. The mesolimbic pathway is the reward pathway, and too much dopamine there is linked to hallucinations and delusions. Blocking it is exactly what the drug is meant to do. The question asks about the side effect, and movement problems come from the nigrostriatal pathway.

p: Dopamine travels along several separate pathways, and each does a different job. The nigrostriatal pathway (substantia nigra to striatum) controls movement. The mesolimbic pathway handles reward. The mesocortical pathway feeds the prefrontal cortex for thinking and motivation. The tuberoinfundibular pathway keeps prolactin low.

A drug that blocks D₂ receptors hits all four at once. So match the symptom to the pathway: shaking and stiffness mean nigrostriatal, high prolactin means tuberoinfundibular, and fewer hallucinations means mesolimbic.

mem: Nigrostriatal: movement (Parkinson's)
Mesolimbic: reward and hallucinations
Mesocortical: thinking and motivation
Tuberoinfundibular: prolactin
x7A_002.trap: Picking mesolimbic because that's the pathway antipsychotics are aimed at. The question asks about the side effect, and the side effect is movement.
x7A_002.plain: Cutting the town's main power line to fix one building also shuts off the lights in the dance studio. The dancers start stumbling, and that tells you which line went down.

ox: Not quite. The parietal lobe, toward the top and back of the head, handles touch and your sense of where things are in space. Damage there can cause neglect, where a person ignores one side of the world, not impulsive or rude behavior.
Not quite. The medulla oblongata, at the base of the brain, controls breathing and heart rate. A rod through it would most likely kill the person, not just change his personality.

Correct. The prefrontal cortex sits at the very front of the brain and handles planning, impulse control and social judgment. Damage there, as in Phineas Gage, leaves a person smart but impulsive and socially out of line.

Not quite. The temporal lobe, on the sides of the head near the ears, handles hearing, understanding language and forming memories. Damage there would show up as trouble with words or memory, not as rude, impulsive behavior.

p: The prefrontal cortex is the front part of the frontal lobe, right behind your forehead. Psychologists call its work executive function: planning ahead, making decisions and stopping yourself from doing things that don't fit the situation.

Phineas Gage showed how this works. After an iron rod passed through his frontal lobe, he could still talk, remember and reason, but he became impulsive, used crude language and couldn't stick to plans. His friends said he was 'no longer Gage.'

mem: Prefrontal cortex: planning, impulse control, social judgment
Phineas Gage: frontal damage, personality change
Parietal: touch and space; temporal: hearing, language, memory
x7A_007.trap: Picking the temporal lobe just because it's another region you know. Changes in impulse control and social behavior point to the front of the brain.
x7A_007.plain: The prefrontal cortex is a car's brakes. Without them the engine still runs fine, but you can't stop yourself.

fig.cap: Each hemisphere receives the opposite visual field. With the corpus callosum cut, the speaking left hemisphere cannot name what only the right saw.
fig.alt: Split-brain experiment with an image in the left visual field.
fig.credit: This diagram was originally developed for the 520 Quest app.

ox: Not quite. Cutting the corpus callosum doesn't blind anyone. The eyes and the visual cortex still work, and the image travels to the right hemisphere as usual. The only problem is that the right half can't share what it saw with the left half.

Correct. The left visual field goes to the right hemisphere. In most people the right hemisphere can't produce speech, so the patient can't name the key. But the right hemisphere controls the left hand, so the left hand can find the key by touch.

Not quite. Naming the key needs the left hemisphere, where speech usually lives, and the right hand is also controlled by the left hemisphere. The left hemisphere never saw the image, so neither of these works.
Not quite. This gets it backward. Naming needs the left hemisphere, and the left hemisphere never got the image. The right hemisphere did see it, so the left hand can still pick out the key.

p: The corpus callosum is a thick bundle of nerve fibers that connects the left and right halves (hemispheres) of the brain. Doctors sometimes cut it to stop severe seizures from spreading. After that, the two halves can't share information.

Three facts let you solve any split-brain question. Each visual field goes to the opposite hemisphere: left field to right brain. Each hemisphere controls the opposite hand: right brain runs the left hand. And in most people, speech sits in the left hemisphere. Trace the path through those three and the answer falls out.

mem: Left visual field goes to the right hemisphere
Speech is usually in the left hemisphere
Each hemisphere controls the opposite hand
x7A_010.trap: Mixing up sides. Trace it every time: left field, right brain, left hand, no words.
x7A_010.plain: Picture two offices with the hallway between them walled off. One office saw the memo but has no phone, so all it can do is point.

ox: Not quite. The second finding says winning raises testosterone. Winning is a behavior outcome, so this is direct evidence that behavior can change hormone levels.

Not quite. 'Sole cause' is far too strong. The link between testosterone and dominance is a correlation, and the winning effect shows it runs both ways. Neither finding shows testosterone is the only thing driving aggression.
Correct. Testosterone is linked to dominance-seeking, and winning a competition pushes testosterone up further. Each one affects the other, which is what bidirectional means.
Not quite. Testosterone is present and affects behavior in people of every sex. Nothing in these findings says it matters only in males.

concept.t: Hormones and behavior go both ways
p: It's easy to think hormones only push behavior around. But behavior and experience also change hormone levels. When the influence runs in both directions, it's called a bidirectional relationship.

Testosterone is a good example. Higher levels go along with more dominance-seeking, and winning a contest raises it further while losing tends to lower it. That loop is why you can't name testosterone as the one and only cause of aggression.

mem: Hormones change behavior, and behavior changes hormones
A correlation can't prove a single cause
Winning tends to raise testosterone
x7A_016.trap: Picking 'sole cause.' Words like 'sole,' 'only' and 'never' are red flags on the MCAT.
x7A_016.plain: It's like a thermostat and a room. The thermostat changes the room's heat, and the room's heat changes what the thermostat does next.

fig.cap: Higher MZ than DZ concordance points to genes; MZ concordance well below 100% points to environment.
fig.alt: Schizophrenia concordance in MZ twins, DZ twins and the general population.
fig.credit: This graph was originally developed for the 520 Quest app. Approximate literature values (question data).

ox: Not quite. This is the most common mix-up. Heritability is about differences between people in a group. It makes no sense to split one person's trait into 60% genes and 40% environment, because the two work together inside each person.

Correct. Heritability is the share of the variation (the differences between people) in a population that's linked to genetic differences among them. A value of 0.6 means about 60% of those differences track with genes in that group, at that time.
Not quite. Heritability isn't an inheritance probability like the odds from a Punnett square. It says nothing about whether a particular child will get the trait from a parent.
Not quite. High heritability doesn't mean unchangeable. Height is highly heritable, yet better nutrition made whole populations taller. Heritability can even change if the environment changes.

p: Heritability is a number from 0 to 1. It tells you how much of the differences between people in one group, at one time, is linked to differences in their genes. A value near 0 means the differences mostly come from environment; near 1 means they mostly track with genes.

Keep three limits in mind. It describes a population, never one person. It isn't the chance of inheriting something. And it doesn't mean a trait can't change, because it's measured in one environment and can shift if that environment changes.

mem: Heritability is about groups, not individuals
It describes variation: the differences between people
It can change when the environment changes
High heritability doesn't mean unchangeable
x7A_019.trap: Reading 0.6 as 'my trait is 60% genes.' It's about the differences across a group.
x7A_019.plain: If a class's test score differences are mostly due to how much each kid studied, that tells you about the class. It doesn't tell you what fraction of any one kid's score came from studying.

fig.cap: Higher MZ than DZ concordance points to genes; MZ concordance well below 100% points to environment.
fig.alt: Schizophrenia concordance in MZ twins, DZ twins and the general population.
fig.credit: This graph was originally developed for the 520 Quest app. Approximate literature values (question data).

ox: Not quite. This flips the biology. MZ (identical) twins come from one fertilized egg that splits in two. DZ (fraternal) twins come from two separate eggs, each fertilized by its own sperm.

Correct. If parents, teachers and friends treat identical twins more alike than fraternal twins, some of the identical twins' extra similarity comes from environment. The twin method can't tell that apart from genes, so it credits genes, and heritability is overestimated.
Not quite. Twins raised together share the same home, parents and family life. That shared setting is part of how the study is built.
Not quite. DZ twins share about 50% of the genes that vary between people, the same as ordinary brothers and sisters. It's MZ twins who share about 100%.

p: Twin studies compare identical (MZ) twins, who share about 100% of their genes, with fraternal (DZ) twins, who share about 50%. If MZ pairs are more alike on a trait than DZ pairs, researchers credit that extra similarity to genes.

This only works if both kinds of twins have equally similar environments. That's the equal environments assumption. If identical twins are dressed alike, put in the same classes and spend more time together, part of their sameness comes from environment, and genes get too much credit.

mem: MZ: one egg, about 100% shared genes
DZ: two eggs, about 50% shared genes
If MZ twins are treated more alike, heritability is overestimated
x7A_021.trap: Picking a genetics statement that just sounds off. The flaw the question wants is about environment, not DNA.
x7A_021.plain: If the twins who look identical also get treated like copies, you can't tell whether their sameness comes from their genes or from how everyone treats them.

ox: Not quite. Evocative correlation is when a person's traits bring out certain responses from others, like a smiley baby getting more smiles back. In this question nobody is reacting to the child; the child is going out and finding social situations.
Not quite. Epigenetics means chemical tags on DNA that turn genes on or off without changing the DNA sequence. It's about how genes are read, not about which situations a child seeks out.

Not quite. Passive correlation is when parents hand down both genes and an environment that matches them, like musical parents who also fill the house with instruments. The child isn't doing anything here. In this question, the child is actively choosing.

Correct. Active gene-environment correlation, or niche-picking, is when people seek out environments that match their inherited tendencies. The sociable child chooses social settings, and those settings build their social skills even more.

p: Gene-environment correlation means genes help shape the environment a person experiences. It's not genes OR environment; the two get tangled together.

Passive: parents supply both the genes and the home, so they match without the child doing anything. Evocative: a child's traits pull certain reactions from others. Active: the person picks settings that fit their traits. Active becomes more important as kids get older and can choose for themselves.

mem: Passive: parents supply genes and environment
Evocative: your traits draw reactions from others
Active: you choose your niche
Epigenetics: switching genes on or off, not changing DNA
x7A_023.trap: Mixing up active and evocative. Ask who's doing the work: if the person chooses, it's active; if others react, it's evocative.
x7A_023.plain: A kid who loves music joins the school band, practices with friends, and gets even better at music.

ox: Not quite. Parkinson disease also involves the basal ganglia, which makes it tempting. But it causes slowed movement, stiffness and a resting tremor from losing dopamine neurons in the substantia nigra. It isn't caused by a CAG repeat, and its movements aren't jerky and dance-like.
Not quite. Multiple sclerosis is an autoimmune disease: the immune system attacks myelin, the fatty coating that helps nerve signals travel. It isn't caused by a repeated stretch of DNA.
Not quite. Alzheimer disease mainly causes memory loss that slowly gets worse. It doesn't cause the jerky movements here, and it isn't a CAG repeat disorder.
Correct. Huntington disease is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by too many CAG repeats in one gene. Neurons in the striatum die, causing chorea (jerky movements), mood changes and dementia.

p: Huntington disease is a genetic disorder caused by too many copies of the three-letter DNA code CAG in a row in one gene. This is called a trinucleotide repeat expansion. It's autosomal dominant, so one copy of the faulty gene from either parent is enough.

The extra repeats damage neurons in the striatum, part of the basal ganglia, which helps smooth out movement. As these cells die, people develop chorea (involuntary jerky movements), mood and personality changes, and a decline in thinking. Symptoms usually start in middle adulthood.

mem: Huntington: CAG repeat, autosomal dominant
Symptoms: jerky movements, mood changes, dementia
Parkinson's: slow movement and resting tremor from dopamine loss
x7A_028.trap: Picking Parkinson's because both are movement disorders. A CAG repeat plus jerky movements means Huntington.
x7A_028.plain: It's like a word that got copy-pasted too many times in a recipe. Past a certain point, the recipe stops working.

ox: Not quite. Neurogenesis means growing new neurons. It doesn't clear amyloid plaques, the protein clumps seen in Alzheimer disease. And the question says the brain damage at autopsy was the same, so nothing was reversed.
Not quite. Retrograde amnesia is losing memories from before an injury. It describes a type of memory loss, not a brain that's better at handling damage.
Correct. Cognitive reserve means education and mental activity build richer brain networks that can handle damage. The disease is just as bad, but symptoms show up later or more mildly.
Not quite. Diagnostic overshadowing is when a doctor blames new symptoms on a diagnosis the patient already has and misses the real cause. It doesn't explain why some people have fewer symptoms.

p: Cognitive reserve is the brain's ability to cope with damage and keep working. Education, mentally challenging jobs, learning new skills and staying socially active all seem to build richer networks of connections.

With more reserve, the brain can reroute around damaged areas. So two people can have the same disease changes in their brains but very different symptoms. Reserve doesn't stop the disease; it delays when the damage starts to show.

mem: Cognitive reserve: resilience built by education and mental activity
Same damage, fewer symptoms
It works around damage; it doesn't remove plaques
x7A_031.trap: Picking neurogenesis because it sounds like repair. The brain works around the damage; it doesn't erase it.
x7A_031.plain: A city with lots of roads can handle a closed street; traffic just takes another route. A town with one road gets stuck.

ox: Correct. Walter Mischel argued that traits predict how someone will act in a given situation only weakly, because behavior changes a lot from one setting to another. That started the person-situation debate.
Not quite. Raymond Cattell built a trait model with 16 personality factors. He was on the side of traits, not one of their critics.
Not quite. Hans Eysenck described broad trait dimensions, like extraversion, and linked them to biology. He defended traits rather than attacking them.
Not quite. Abraham Maslow was a humanistic theorist known for the hierarchy of needs and self-actualization. He wasn't the critic in the trait debate.

p: Trait theories say stable personality traits explain how people behave. Walter Mischel noticed that people act quite differently in different settings, so a trait score predicts any single behavior poorly. He argued the situation matters more than trait theorists admitted.

The modern view is interactionist: both the person and the situation matter. Traits predict behavior well when averaged over many situations, and people show steady 'if this situation, then that behavior' patterns.

mem: Mischel: critic of traits, stressed the situation
Cattell: 16 factors; Eysenck: biological trait dimensions
Maslow: humanistic, hierarchy of needs
Modern view: interactionist
x7A_046.trap: Picking a famous trait theorist. The critic is the one who stressed the situation.
x7A_046.plain: A kid can be loud at recess and quiet in class. Calling them just 'loud' misses the fact that the setting changes how they act.

ox: Not quite. Eysenck's theory was built around the reticular activating system, which controls overall alertness. The size of the amygdala wasn't part of his explanation.
Not quite. Eysenck didn't blame introversion on extra dopamine in the striatum. His theory was about baseline cortical arousal.
Correct. Introverts already have higher baseline cortical arousal. A loud party adds even more stimulation and pushes them past a comfortable level, so they avoid it.
Not quite. This is the reversal trap. Low baseline arousal is how Eysenck explained extraverts: they start low, so they seek out parties and excitement to reach a comfortable level.

p: Eysenck said introverts and extraverts differ in baseline cortical arousal, meaning how alert the brain is at rest. He linked this to the reticular activating system in the brainstem.

Everyone has a comfortable level of arousal. Introverts start high, so extra stimulation feels like too much and they avoid it. Extraverts start low, so they seek out noise, people and excitement to get up to that comfortable level.

mem: Introvert: high baseline arousal, avoids stimulation
Extravert: low baseline arousal, seeks stimulation
Based on the reticular activating system
x7A_048.trap: Flipping the two types. Introverts are already full, so they avoid more.
x7A_048.plain: If your cup is already almost full, you don't want more water poured in. If it's nearly empty, you want a lot.

ox: Not quite. Social cognitive researchers look at beliefs like self-efficacy (your confidence that you can do something) and what you expect will happen, usually through questionnaires. It's tempting because telling a story involves thinking, but they aren't hunting for unconscious motives.

Correct. Projective tests such as the TAT and the Rorschach give a vague image and let the person fill in the meaning. The idea is that hidden, unconscious motives leak into the story. That belief in a powerful unconscious comes from Freud's psychoanalytic tradition.

Not quite. Trait researchers use structured self-report questionnaires with fixed items, such as the NEO-PI, which measures the Big Five traits. Both are 'personality tests,' but trait tests ask everyone the same questions and score them the same way. They aren't open-ended.
Not quite. Behaviorists study what people actually do and what follows it, like rewards and punishments. They don't try to read hidden motives out of a story about a picture.

concept.t: Projective tests and the psychoanalytic view
p: A projective test shows something vague, like an inkblot or an unclear picture, and asks the person to interpret it. 'Projecting' means putting your own inner feelings onto something outside you.

Psychoanalytic theory, started by Freud, says much of the mind is unconscious, out of our awareness. A vague image gives those hidden motives a chance to show up. Other approaches use other tools: trait theorists use fixed questionnaires, and social cognitive theorists measure beliefs and expectations.

mem: Projective tests (TAT, Rorschach): psychoanalytic
Trait: fixed self-report questionnaires (NEO-PI, Big Five)
Social cognitive: self-efficacy and expectations
x7A_054.trap: Calling every personality test 'trait.' A vague picture plus an open-ended answer means the test is after unconscious motives, so pick psychoanalytic.
x7A_054.plain: It's like seeing shapes in the clouds. What you see says something about what's already on your mind.

ox: Not quite. Gray matter is the tissue that holds the bodies of nerve cells. In schizophrenia it tends to be reduced, especially in the temporal and frontal lobes. This choice gets the direction backward.

Correct. Ventricles are fluid-filled spaces in the brain. When the surrounding brain tissue shrinks, the ventricles look larger. Enlarged lateral and third ventricles are the most often repeated structural finding in schizophrenia.

Not quite. The corpus callosum is the bundle of fibers that connects the two halves of the brain. Being born without one is a rare developmental condition, and it isn't a typical finding in schizophrenia.

Not quite. Schizophrenia is linked to lower activity in the frontal lobes, called hypofrontality, not bigger frontal lobes. That lower activity fits the trouble with planning and flat emotion many patients have.

p: Schizophrenia is a serious mental illness with hallucinations, delusions and disorganized thinking. On brain scans, it usually shows a loss of brain tissue. Gray matter is reduced, so the fluid-filled ventricles grow to fill the space.

Frontal lobe activity is also lower, which is called hypofrontality. That fits the negative symptoms, like flat emotion and poor motivation. Positive symptoms, like hallucinations, are linked to too much dopamine activity.

mem: Enlarged ventricles: the most consistent finding
Less gray matter and lower frontal activity
Positive symptoms tie to excess dopamine
x7A_064.trap: Choices that say tissue is 'increased' or 'enlarged.' In schizophrenia, brain tissue goes down and ventricles go up.
x7A_064.plain: If you take some rocks out of a full fish tank, there's more room for water. Less brain tissue leaves bigger fluid spaces.

fig.cap: Higher MZ than DZ concordance points to genes; MZ concordance well below 100% points to environment.
fig.alt: Schizophrenia concordance in MZ twins, DZ twins and the general population.
fig.credit: This graph was originally developed for the 520 Quest app. Approximate literature values (question data).

ox: Not quite. Identical twins have nearly the same DNA. If schizophrenia were entirely genetic, when one twin had it, the other would almost always have it too, close to 100%. A rate of 45% is far below that, so genes can't be the whole story.

Not quite. Identical twins match 45% of the time and fraternal twins 15%. That's 3 times as often (15 × 3 = 45). The more genes twins share, the more often they match, which is clear evidence that genes play a role.

Correct. MZ twins share nearly all their genes and DZ twins about half. MZ concordance being higher (45% vs 15%) shows genes contribute. MZ concordance being well under 100% shows non-genetic factors matter too. That's the diathesis-stress idea: vulnerability plus stress.

Not quite. Both kinds of twins raised together share a family environment about equally. If shared family life were the main cause, MZ and DZ twins would match at about the same rate. Instead it's 45% vs 15%, so the family home can't be the main explanation.

p: Concordance is the chance that if one twin has a condition, the other twin has it too. Identical (MZ) twins share about 100% of their genes, and fraternal (DZ) twins share about 50%.

Two comparisons tell you two things. If MZ concordance is higher than DZ, genes play a role. If MZ concordance is below 100%, environment plays a role too, because two people with the same genes still turned out differently.
This pattern fits the diathesis-stress model. A diathesis is a built-in vulnerability, often genetic. It only turns into illness when stress, like trauma or drug use, pushes on it.

mem: MZ above DZ: genes matter
MZ below 100%: environment matters
Diathesis-stress: vulnerability plus a stressor
x7A_065.sc: Compare MZ to DZ to see if genes matter. Compare MZ to 100% to see if environment matters.
x7A_065.trap: Extreme answers like 'entirely genetic' or 'no role' are usually wrong. When MZ is above DZ but below 100%, pick the balanced answer.
x7A_065.plain: Identical twins have the same recipe, but they don't always bake the same cake. Something in the kitchen made a difference.

ox: Not quite. Phobias are explained mainly by classical conditioning, where something gets paired with a scary event, and then avoidance keeps the fear going. Learned helplessness is about giving up, not about being afraid.
Not quite. Schizophrenia involves psychosis: hallucinations, delusions and disorganized thinking. Learned helplessness doesn't model any of those.

Not quite. In OCD, a person has unwanted thoughts (obsessions) and does repeated rituals (compulsions) to ease the anxiety. The dogs weren't doing rituals. They were doing nothing at all, which is passivity.

Correct. The dogs learned that their actions didn't stop the shocks, so they quit trying even when escape was easy. That passivity and hopelessness looks like depression, so learned helplessness is a classic model of major depressive disorder.

p: Learned helplessness happens when repeated bad events that you can't control teach you that your actions don't matter. After that, you stop trying, even when you actually could fix things.

Seligman showed this with dogs and then linked it to depression. People with depression often feel they have no control over what happens to them, so they become passive and hopeless. Later versions of the theory added that how people explain their failures matters too.

mem: Seligman: learned helplessness
Can't escape shocks, then stops trying to escape
Used as a model of depression
x7A_074.trap: Linking it to phobias just because shocks are scary. The key behavior is giving up, not fear.
x7A_074.plain: If you fail a class no matter how hard you study, you might stop studying, even for a test that would have been easy.

ox: Not quite. Behavioral models say depression comes from too little positive reinforcement: fewer good things happen, so the person does less, and even fewer good things happen. 'Too much' reinforcement is backward, and it isn't Beck's cognitive view.
Not quite. The psychoanalytic view, from Freud, described depression as anger turned inward against the self, not outward. Either way, it's a different theory from Beck's.

Not quite. Too much dopamine in the mesolimbic pathway is the dopamine hypothesis of schizophrenia and psychosis. Biological theories of depression point more to serotonin and norepinephrine, and Beck's theory is about thoughts, not chemicals.
Correct. Beck's cognitive triad is negative views of the self, the world and the future. Distorted thinking keeps those views alive, and those thoughts keep the depression going.

p: Beck noticed that depressed people think in a predictable pattern he called the cognitive triad: 'I'm worthless' (self), 'the world is against me' (world), and 'it will never get better' (future).

Cognitive distortions are thinking errors that keep this going. Overgeneralization turns one failure into 'I fail at everything.' Cognitive therapy teaches people to spot these thoughts and test them against the facts.

mem: Cognitive triad: self, world, future
Beck: cognitive therapy
Freud: anger turned inward
x7A_075.mn: Self, World, Future: the three things a depressed mind sees in gray. Think 'S-W-F.'
x7A_075.trap: Mixing up Beck (thoughts) with Freud (anger turned inward) or the dopamine hypothesis (psychosis).
x7A_075.plain: It's like wearing gray-tinted glasses. You, the world and tomorrow all look gloomy, and the glasses stay on until someone points them out.

ox: Not quite. Extinction is when a learned response fades because the trigger stops being followed by the outcome. It makes responses weaker. It can't build a brand new fear.

Correct. The dog started as a neutral stimulus. The bite was an unconditioned stimulus, meaning it causes fear without any learning. Pairing the two turned dogs into a conditioned stimulus, and fear of dogs is now the conditioned response. Fearing every dog shows generalization.

Not quite. Observational learning means learning by watching what happens to other people. It can create phobias, but she was bitten herself, so direct classical conditioning explains how her fear started.

Not quite. Latent learning is learning that stays hidden until there's a reason to show it, like a rat that learns a maze without reward and runs it fast once food appears. It doesn't explain a fear that shows up right after a bite.

concept.t: How classical conditioning creates a phobia
p: In classical conditioning, a neutral stimulus is paired with an unconditioned stimulus, something that triggers a reaction without any learning (a bite causes pain and fear). After pairing, the neutral stimulus triggers a similar reaction by itself. It's now a conditioned stimulus, and the reaction is a conditioned response.

Here, dog plus bite leads to dog alone causing fear. When the fear spreads to all dogs, not just the one that bit her, that's stimulus generalization. What keeps the phobia going later is avoidance, which is a different kind of learning.

mem: Neutral stimulus + unconditioned stimulus makes a conditioned stimulus
Phobia onset: classical conditioning
Generalization: similar things trigger the same fear
x7A_078.trap: Picking observational learning because it's a known path to phobias. If she was bitten directly, it's classical conditioning.
x7A_078.plain: A kid touches a hot stove right as the kitchen timer dings, a few times in a row. Soon the ding alone makes the kid flinch.

ox: Not quite. Spontaneous recovery is when a response that had faded (been extinguished) suddenly comes back after a rest period. Avoidance isn't what causes that.

Correct. Avoiding the feared object brings relief. Taking away something unpleasant is negative reinforcement, so the avoidance becomes more likely next time. And because the person never faces the object, the fear never gets the chance to fade.

Not quite. Punishment makes a behavior less likely. Here avoidance becomes more common over time, so it's being reinforced, not punished. Removing the bad feeling of anxiety is negative reinforcement.
Not quite. This is backward. Extinction requires facing the feared object and seeing that nothing bad happens. Avoidance prevents exactly that, so it keeps the fear alive.

concept.t: Why avoidance keeps a phobia going
p: Mowrer's two-factor theory says phobias use two kinds of learning. First, classical conditioning creates the fear by pairing something with a bad experience. Second, operant conditioning keeps it going: avoiding the thing makes the anxiety drop, and that relief rewards the avoidance.

Taking away something unpleasant to make a behavior more likely is called negative reinforcement. 'Negative' means removing, not 'bad.' This is why exposure therapy works: facing the fear safely lets it finally fade.

mem: Negative reinforcement: remove something unpleasant, behavior goes up
Avoidance blocks extinction
Exposure therapy treats phobias
x7A_079.trap: Calling negative reinforcement a kind of punishment. Reinforcement always makes behavior more likely; punishment makes it less likely.
x7A_079.plain: If you skip the dentist because it scares you, the relief feels great, so you skip again. The fear never gets a chance to shrink.

ox: Not quite. Generalized anxiety disorder, which is constant worry about many things, stayed in the anxiety disorders class in DSM-5. OCD was the one that moved out.
Not quite. PTSD did move out of the anxiety disorders in DSM-5, which makes this tempting. But it went to the trauma- and stressor-related disorders class, not to the same class as OCD.

Correct. DSM-5 created a class called obsessive-compulsive and related disorders. It includes OCD, body dysmorphic disorder, hoarding disorder, trichotillomania (hair pulling) and excoriation (skin picking), which all involve repeated thoughts or behaviors that are hard to stop.
Not quite. Panic disorder, with its sudden waves of intense fear, is still an anxiety disorder in DSM-5.

p: The DSM-5 groups disorders into classes based on shared features. In 2013 it pulled OCD out of the anxiety disorders and gave it its own class: obsessive-compulsive and related disorders.

The members all involve repeated, hard-to-stop thoughts or actions: OCD, body dysmorphic disorder (worrying about a perceived flaw in how you look), hoarding, trichotillomania (pulling out hair) and excoriation (picking skin). PTSD also left the anxiety class, but into trauma- and stressor-related disorders.

mem: OCD, body dysmorphic disorder, hoarding, hair pulling, skin picking: one class
PTSD: trauma- and stressor-related
GAD and panic: still anxiety disorders
x7A_081.trap: Both OCD and PTSD left the anxiety class, so it's easy to put them together. They went to different classes.
x7A_081.plain: DSM-5 reorganized the closet. OCD got its own shelf, shared with other habits of repeated thoughts and actions.

ox: Not quite. Illness anxiety disorder is constant worry about having or getting a serious illness, with few or no actual symptoms. She doesn't seem worried about being sick; she suddenly can't move her arm.
Not quite. In factitious disorder, a person fakes or causes their own symptoms on purpose so they can be seen as sick. Nothing here suggests she is doing this on purpose.

Not quite. Somatic symptom disorder is about too many thoughts, feelings and worries about physical symptoms. The key feature here is different: a sudden loss of movement that doesn't match any nerve disease.

Correct. Conversion disorder (functional neurological symptom disorder) is a real motor or sensory symptom, like paralysis, with normal neurological tests. It often follows stress, and the person isn't faking it.

p: Conversion disorder means a real symptom that looks like a nerve problem, such as paralysis, blindness or numbness, but doesn't match any known disease. Tests come back normal. It often appears after psychological stress, which is where the old idea of stress being 'converted' into a body symptom comes from.
The person isn't faking. Faking on purpose to be seen as sick is factitious disorder. Faking for an outside reward, like money or getting out of work, is malingering.

mem: Sudden motor or sensory loss + normal tests + stress: conversion
Not done on purpose
Illness anxiety: worry with few symptoms
x7A_088.trap: Picking somatic symptom disorder just because the symptom is physical. Worry about symptoms points to somatic symptom disorder; a sudden loss of function points to conversion.
x7A_088.plain: It's like a smoke alarm going off when there's no fire. The alarm is really ringing, but the wiring checks out fine.

ox: Correct. Somatic symptom disorder means one or more distressing physical symptoms plus too many thoughts, feelings or behaviors about them. The pain can be real. The problem is how much the worry takes over.

Not quite. This is the tempting choice, since her worry feels like anxiety. But DSM-5 puts worry that centers on bodily symptoms into the somatic symptom and related disorders class, not the anxiety disorders.
Not quite. Dissociative disorders involve a break in memory, identity or awareness, like losing chunks of time. She has none of these.
Not quite. Neurocognitive disorders involve a decline in thinking or memory, like dementia or delirium. Nothing suggests her thinking is getting worse.

p: In somatic symptom disorder, a person has bodily symptoms and spends an outsized amount of time and energy worrying about them. The worry is out of proportion to how serious the symptoms are.

The symptoms can be real, like pain, and they don't have to be medically unexplained. Compare its neighbors in the same DSM-5 class: illness anxiety disorder is worry about being sick with few or no symptoms, and conversion disorder is a sudden nerve-type symptom with no disease behind it.

mem: Somatic symptom disorder: real symptom + too much worry
Illness anxiety: worry with few symptoms
Conversion: nerve-type loss with no disease found
x7A_090.trap: Picking anxiety disorders because of all the worry. When the worry is about body symptoms, pick somatic symptom disorder.
x7A_090.plain: It's like checking a small scratch hundreds of times a day. The scratch is real, but the worry has taken over your day.

ox: Not quite. Dependent personality disorder means clinging, giving in to others and needing to be taken care of. It doesn't include the fast swing from idealizing someone to hating them.

Correct. Borderline personality disorder involves unstable relationships, self-image and emotions, a strong fear of abandonment, self-harm, and splitting: seeing people as all good or all bad and switching quickly between the two.
Not quite. Histrionic personality disorder is about needing to be the center of attention and showing big, dramatic emotions. Self-harm and splitting aren't its core features.

Not quite. Bipolar II has periods of mild mania (hypomania) and depression that each last days to weeks. Borderline mood shifts happen within hours and track what's going on in relationships, which fits this woman better.

p: A personality disorder is a long-lasting pattern of thinking and behaving that causes problems in life. Borderline personality disorder shows instability everywhere: in relationships, in sense of self, and in mood. Impulsive actions and self-harm are common, often driven by fear of being abandoned.

Splitting is its signature. The person sees others as all good (idealizing) or all bad (devaluing) and can flip quickly. Borderline is in Cluster B, the dramatic and emotional group, along with antisocial, histrionic and narcissistic.

mem: Splitting: idealize, then devalue
Fear of abandonment and self-harm
Cluster B personality disorder
x7A_093.trap: Mood swings pull you toward bipolar. Bipolar episodes last days to weeks; borderline shifts last hours and follow relationship events.
x7A_093.plain: A friend who calls you their hero on Monday and their worst enemy on Tuesday, with nothing in between.

ox: Correct. Avoidant personality disorder means wanting relationships but holding back because of fear of criticism and rejection, along with feeling inadequate. That matches a man who longs for friends but keeps away.
Not quite. Paranoid personality disorder involves distrust and suspicion: the person assumes others mean them harm. He isn't suspicious; he's afraid of being rejected.
Not quite. Antisocial personality disorder involves lying, breaking rules and ignoring other people's rights without guilt. It has nothing to do with fearing rejection.

Not quite. Schizoid personality disorder also leads to few relationships, which is why it's tempting. But schizoid people genuinely don't want close ties and show little emotion. This man desperately wants friends.

p: Avoidant and schizoid people both end up with few relationships, so look at the reason. Avoidant: wants connection, but fear of rejection keeps them away. Schizoid: doesn't really care about connection.
They sit in different clusters. Avoidant is in Cluster C, the anxious and fearful group. Schizoid is in Cluster A, the odd and eccentric group, along with paranoid.

mem: Avoidant: wants friends, fears rejection (Cluster C)
Schizoid: not interested in friends (Cluster A)
Paranoid: suspicious of others (Cluster A)
x7A_095.sc: Ask one question: does he want friends? Yes means avoidant. No means schizoid.
x7A_095.trap: Both have few friends. The deciding detail is whether the person wants them.
x7A_095.plain: Avoidant is the kid who wants to join the game but is too scared to ask. Schizoid is the kid who'd honestly rather play alone.

ox: Not quite. Intrusive thoughts that the person finds unwanted and tries to resist are OCD obsessions. That's ego-dystonic, and it's exactly what OCPD lacks.

Correct. OCPD is a lasting style of perfectionism, orderliness and control that the person sees as correct (ego-syntonic). There are no true obsessions. In OCD, the obsessions feel unwanted (ego-dystonic).
Not quite. There's no rule that one is always more disabling than the other. How much either one gets in the way of life varies a lot from person to person.
Not quite. Psychotic disorders involve losing touch with reality, like hallucinations. OCPD is a personality disorder, and the person stays fully in touch with reality.

p: OCD has obsessions (unwanted, intrusive thoughts) and compulsions (rituals done to ease the anxiety). The person usually knows these are excessive and finds them distressing. That's called ego-dystonic: the symptoms feel foreign, not part of who you are.

OCPD is a personality style that lasts a lifetime: perfectionism, rules, lists and control. The person thinks this is just the correct way to live. That's ego-syntonic: it feels like part of the self. So people with OCPD rarely see a problem; they think everyone else is too sloppy.

mem: OCD: ego-dystonic (unwanted)
OCPD: ego-syntonic, no true obsessions
They can occur together
x7A_096.mn: Syntonic sounds like 'in sync': in sync with the self. Dystonic is out of sync.
x7A_096.trap: The names are almost the same. Ask whether the person sees the behavior as unwanted (OCD) or as simply right (OCPD).
x7A_096.plain: OCD is a song stuck in your head that you hate. OCPD is insisting your way of folding towels is the correct way, and being annoyed that others don't see it.

ox: Not quite. People with anxiety disorders usually find their worry and fear unwanted and upsetting. That's ego-dystonic, the opposite of what this patient shows.
Not quite. Dissociative identity disorder, where a person has two or more distinct identities, usually involves confusion, memory gaps and real distress.
Correct. Personality disorder traits are usually ego-syntonic. They feel like a natural part of who the person is, so the person feels little distress and may blame others when there's conflict.
Not quite. Depression involves deep sadness and distress that the person clearly feels and doesn't want. That's ego-dystonic.

p: Ego-syntonic means a trait feels in tune with who you are. The person sees it as 'just me' or 'the right way.' Ego-dystonic means the opposite: the symptom feels foreign and unwanted.

Personality disorders are usually ego-syntonic, which is why people with them often don't seek help on their own. Most other disorders, like anxiety, depression and OCD, are ego-dystonic: they hurt, and the person wants them gone.

mem: Personality disorders: ego-syntonic
Anxiety, depression, OCD: ego-dystonic
Low distress means fewer people seek treatment
x7A_098.trap: Low distress about rigid traits points to a personality disorder, not a mood or anxiety disorder.
x7A_098.plain: A kid who thinks being bossy is just being right won't ask for help changing. A kid with a stomachache will.

ox: Not quite. Delirium is a neurocognitive disorder, meaning a problem with thinking and awareness. A personality disorder is a lifelong pattern, not something that appears suddenly after a new drug.
Not quite. Delirium is often reversible. Once the cause, like a medication, infection or metabolic problem, is fixed, the confusion often clears.
Correct. Delirium starts over hours to days, attention swings up and down, and there's a cause you can find. It often reverses. Dementia develops gradually and keeps getting worse.
Not quite. Impaired attention is the main feature of delirium, and the question says her attention changes hour to hour. Memory loss with steady attention sounds more like early dementia.

p: Delirium is a sudden disturbance in attention and awareness that comes and goes during the day. Common causes are medications, infections and metabolic problems. It's very common in older adults in the hospital, and it often clears when the cause is treated.

Dementia, like Alzheimer disease, is a slow, steady decline in memory and thinking over months to years. Attention is usually fairly normal early on. Sudden and swinging means delirium; slow and steady means dementia.

mem: Delirium: sudden, swinging attention, often reversible
Dementia: gradual and progressive
Delirium is common in hospitalized older adults
x7A_100.trap: Picking 'memory loss only.' Delirium is mainly an attention problem that comes on suddenly.
x7A_100.plain: Delirium is a sudden storm that can blow over. Dementia is a coastline slowly wearing away.

ox: Not quite. Spontaneous recovery is when a conditioned response that had faded suddenly returns after a rest period. Here the drawing fell below its original level, which is the opposite of something coming back.

Correct. In the overjustification effect, an expected outside reward for something people already enjoy makes them credit the reward for their behavior. When the reward stops, their own motivation is lower than before.
Not quite. Learned helplessness comes from repeated bad events a person can't control, which teaches them to stop trying. Getting paid for drawing isn't a bad, uncontrollable event.
Not quite. Drive reduction theory says we act to satisfy body needs, like eating when hungry. Drawing doesn't fill a biological need, so this theory doesn't explain the drop.

p: Intrinsic motivation is doing something because you enjoy it for its own sake. Extrinsic motivation is doing something to get a reward or avoid a punishment.

When you pay someone for an activity they already love, they may start to explain their behavior by the pay: 'I draw because I get paid.' Take away the pay and the reason seems gone, so they do it less than before. The effect is strongest when the reward is expected and tied to doing the task.

mem: Overjustification: outside reward lowers inner motivation
Happens with activities people already enjoy
Drive reduction: body needs like hunger
x7A_110.trap: Picking spontaneous recovery. That's a conditioned response coming back, not motivation dropping.
x7A_110.plain: A kid who loves reading gets paid a dollar per book. When the dollars stop, reading starts to feel like an unpaid job, so the kid reads less.

fig.cap: A drug's effect triggers an opposing process that strengthens with repetition: tolerance during use, stronger withdrawal after.
fig.alt: Net feeling over time for first and repeated drug exposures.
fig.credit: This graph was originally developed for the 520 Quest app. Schematic curves.

ox: Not quite. This describes incentive theory, where outside rewards pull behavior. It's a real motivation theory, but it doesn't explain why the high shrinks and the crash grows over time.

Correct. A drug causes a first reaction, the high. The brain answers with an opposite reaction to restore balance. With repeated use, the opposite reaction gets stronger, so the high shrinks (tolerance) and the low after the drug wears off gets worse (withdrawal).
Not quite. The theory says the opposing reaction grows with repeated use, not that cells die after one dose. Watch out for words like 'permanently' and the idea of one-time damage.
Not quite. The whole theory is about emotion shifting first one way and then the opposite way. If arousal stayed constant, there would be no tolerance and no withdrawal to explain.

p: Opponent-process theory says your body likes to stay balanced. When something triggers a strong feeling, like a drug high, the brain starts an opposite feeling to pull you back toward normal.

With repeated use, that opposite feeling shows up faster and gets stronger. Tolerance means the same dose gives less of a high, because the opposite reaction cancels more of it. Withdrawal means the opposite feeling is left over after the drug is gone, and wanting to escape that low keeps people using.

mem: A first reaction is followed by an opposite reaction (Solomon)
Repetition makes the opposite reaction stronger
Stronger opposite reaction: tolerance and withdrawal
Incentive theory: outside rewards, a different idea
x7A_115.trap: Mixing up opponent-process with incentive theory or drive reduction. Look for 'an opposite reaction that grows with repetition.'
x7A_115.plain: Think of a seesaw. Each time someone pushes one end up, the other end learns to push back harder. Soon the same push barely lifts it, and the drop afterward is bigger.

fig.cap: ELM: central route (argument quality) when motivated and able, peripheral route (cues) otherwise. TPB: attitude, subjective norms and perceived control shape intention.
fig.alt: Elaboration likelihood model and theory of planned behavior.
fig.credit: This diagram was originally developed for the 520 Quest app.

ox: Correct. Students were randomly given a side and then argued it. Their attitudes moved toward that side. Acting out a role can change what you believe, through self-perception and through easing the discomfort of cognitive dissonance.
Not quite. Because the sides were assigned at random, the students' existing traits can't explain why their attitudes shifted. 'Fully determine' is also far too strong, a common trap word.
Not quite. Drive reduction theory is about satisfying body needs, like eating to reduce hunger. Arguing a debate side doesn't satisfy a biological need.

p: An attitude is a lasting opinion or feeling about something. People often assume attitudes drive behavior, and they do. But behavior can also shape attitudes.

Role-playing is one example: when you argue for a view or act out a part, you may start to believe it. Self-perception theory says we infer our attitudes from what we see ourselves doing. Cognitive dissonance theory says the clash between what we did and what we believed feels uncomfortable, so we shift the belief to match.

p: This theory predicts what people do by looking at their intention, their plan to do it. Intention depends on three things working together.

Attitude is how you feel about the action. Subjective norms are what the people who matter to you expect you to do. Perceived behavioral control is how confident you feel that you can actually pull it off. The stronger all three are, the stronger the intention, and the more likely the behavior.

p: This model explains how people get persuaded. Elaboration means thinking hard about a message. How much you elaborate depends on how motivated you are and whether you're able to focus.

If you're motivated and able, you take the central route and judge the arguments. If not, you take the peripheral route and get swayed by cues like attractiveness or expertise. Central-route change lasts longer and holds up better against counterarguments.

p: Explicit attitudes are the ones you're aware of and can report. Implicit attitudes are automatic mental links you may not notice or control.

The Implicit Association Test measures how quickly you pair groups with good or bad words. Quicker pairing means a stronger link in your mind. When test results and self-reports disagree, it shows that what people believe they feel and their automatic reactions can be two different things.
